newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK- Focus on Greenspan's remarks.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK- Focus on Greenspan's remarks.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's comments on the state of the economy will preoccupy bond market participants Thursday.

Greenspan testifies before the Senate Finance Committee beginning at 1000 EST/1500 GMT and his remarks will be closely scrutinized for hints on his mindset on inflation before next week's meeting of the Fed's policy- making arm. The only other data on Thursday are initial jobless claims, the help wanted index and the APICS survey, none of which are expected to draw attention from the chairman's remarks.
On Wednesday the Treasury successfully launched its first auction of inflation-indexed bonds, but analysts said it is unlikely it will carry any follow-through implications.
"Remember, this thing is traded in a world of its own. It does not trade in tandem with the rest of the market," said Anthony Karadakis, senior financial economist at First National Bank of Chicago.

Instead, the market will take its cue from Greenspan, although Karadakis was not sure the Fed chairman would really have anything dramatically different to say than the last time he appeared on Capitol Hill.

"It's interesting to note the market's price action since the beginning of December and now. We see some of the classic signs of a bear market setting in," said Kevin Flanagan, economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
"In recent weeks we've had a lot of negative price action as the result of what would normally be seen in the bond market as stronger than expected economic news," Flanagan said.
"Housing starts plunge, the ECI is right where the market would have wanted it a month ago and durable goods come in very weak -- and the result is yields move up a tad," he said.
Now the market seems to ignore what should be considered good economic news for fixed-income securities, he said.

Even if a market friendly initial jobless claims number hits the tape on Thursday morning, it may not have the usual impact. Flanagan also did not believe Greenspan would have much to say to excite the market.
Instead, the GDP's release on Friday could be compelling.

"If we get a 4.0 percent rise in GNP and the market tanks, the Fed's on notice that maybe its policy directives are lagging what the market already was pricing in. It'll hit them right between the eyes," Flanagan said.
Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A., expected an innocuous 5,000 dip in claims and 1-tick rise in the Conference Board's help wanted index would not be market moving Thursday.

"The main event will be Greenspan and it's not so much what he says as much as it is what people read between the lines on what he says," Stiles said. "I'll be curious to see if he says anything about ECI being understated."
Stiles thought Greenspan was more comfortable with long bond yields in the 6.90 percent range than with them hovering around 6.50 percent, providing unnecessary stimulus.
However, he added that Greenspan may shortly be running out of patience if he thought GDP was growing too broadly.
"Inflation is still hard to pinpoint, but clearly he's concerned its out there by the wayside waiting to make its presence felt," Stiles said.

Late Wednesday, the two-year note was 99-23/32, up 2/32, to yield 6.03 percent. The 10-year was up 6/32 at 99-5/32 to yield 6.62 percent. The 30-year bond was up 9/32 at 94-29/32 to yield 6.90 percent. Dealers said Federal funds would open between 5-5/16 percent and 5-3/8 percent Thursday.
